templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. Your shift starts in ten minutes, and you are stuck in traffic that will make you about ten minutes late. You can safely make a hands-free call, and {coworker} is already at work.

options.text: Call your {lead} hands-free right away, say you will be about ten minutes late, and give your expected arrival.
options.why: Telling your {lead} early lets them plan coverage. A specific arrival time shows respect for the team.

options.text: Drive faster to make up the time, and explain when you arrive that traffic was bad.
options.why: Speeding is unsafe, and explaining after the fact leaves no time to plan coverage.
options.misconception: Showing up quickly matters more than telling anyone.

options.text: Text {coworker} to clock you in so that it looks like you arrived on time.
options.why: Asking someone to record time you were not there is dishonest, and it hides the delay from the person responsible for scheduling.
options.misconception: A coworker can cover for me.

options.text: Call in sick, since you will be late anyway and it is simpler than explaining the traffic.
options.why: Claiming illness to avoid explaining is dishonest, and a short delay can be handled openly.
options.misconception: A made-up reason is easier than the truth.

templates.principle: If you will be late, tell the right person as early as is safely possible and give a realistic arrival time.
templates.timing: The shift starts soon, so notification comes before arrival or any other step.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, where employees must wear a name badge while on duty. You realize you left yours at home, and your {lead} is on site.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Tell your {lead} you forgot your badge, and ask how to get a temporary one for the day.
options.why: Meeting the badge expectation matters, and telling your {lead} lets the problem be solved properly with a temporary badge.

options.text: Work without the badge and say nothing, since you are known to everyone on the team.
options.why: The expectation applies to everyone. Being known by the team does not help visitors or people who do not recognize you.
options.misconception: Rules only matter for people who are not known.

options.text: Borrow a coworker's badge for the day, since they are not using it at the moment.
options.why: A badge identifies a particular person, so borrowing one is misleading and can cause problems.
options.misconception: One badge is as good as another.

options.text: Write your name on a piece of tape and stick it on your shirt, and then continue working.
options.why: A homemade label is not the issued badge, and you still have not told anyone who could give you the right one.
options.misconception: Anything that shows my name is good enough.

templates.principle: Meet the workplace's appearance expectations; if you cannot, tell your supervisor and ask for a proper solution.

templates.scenario: In the work group chat for {workplace|the}, {coworker} posts a message that annoys you. You are irritated, and you can see that many coworkers will read whatever you post next.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Wait until you are calm, then reply respectfully in the chat or talk with {coworker} privately.
options.why: Messages in a work chat are seen by many people and stay visible. Waiting and keeping it respectful keeps the focus on the work.

options.text: Post a sarcastic reply right away so that everyone can see how you feel about it.
options.why: A sarcastic reply in front of the group can hurt a working relationship and reflect on you, even if you were right to be annoyed.
options.misconception: Showing my feelings in public is honest and healthy.

options.text: Complain about the message in a separate chat with a few coworkers, instead of in the main group.
options.why: Side chats still leave a written record and can reach people you did not intend. It also does not address the issue with {coworker}.
options.misconception: A private group chat is a safe place to complain.

options.text: Ignore the message entirely and avoid replying to anything {coworker} posts after this.
options.why: Ignoring a person can create tension, and an unresolved work question may be left unanswered.
options.misconception: Ignoring someone is the same as being professional.

templates.principle: Online messages at work are visible and lasting: pause, keep your tone respectful, and use a private conversation when needed.

templates.scenario: You are new at {workplace|the} and a little nervous. {Client|a} arrives and looks around uncertainly while your {lead} is on a call and cannot greet them yet.

options.text: Greet them with eye contact, say your name and role, and ask how you can help while letting your {lead} know.
options.why: A friendly greeting and offer to help makes a visitor feel welcome right away, and letting your {lead} know keeps them informed.

options.text: Smile, tell them your {lead} will be free shortly, and wait for your {lead} to take over.
options.why: This is polite and keeps things moving, but it does not offer help or introduce yourself, so the visitor is left waiting.
options.misconception: Waiting for my supervisor is always safest.

options.text: Keep busy at your desk until your {lead} is free, so that you do not say the wrong thing.
options.why: Ignoring a visitor can feel unwelcoming, and a short friendly greeting is rarely a mistake.
options.misconception: If I am nervous, it is better to stay out of it.

options.text: Tell them your {lead} is busy and suggest they come back at a better time.
options.why: Sending a visitor away without checking could lose them and sounds dismissive. They may be happy to wait if welcomed.

templates.principle: Represent your workplace by greeting people, introducing yourself, and offering help, even when you are new or nervous.

review.notes: Acceptable option is courteous but passive.

templates.scenario: An employee writes this request to their {lead}.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is a problem.

segments.whyFine: A greeting is a normal way to begin.

segments.text: I would like to request next Friday off for a family event.
segments.whyFine: A clear, specific request stating the day and reason.

segments.text: Give me an answer today, or I will just not come in.
segments.why: This is a demand with a threat, which is not an appropriate way to ask for time off.

templates.principle: Make requests politely and professionally; demands and threats damage trust.

templates.scenario: You have a job interview next week at {workplace|a}.
templates.prompt: Put these preparation steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Research the workplace and the role
Plan what to wear and how to get there
Arrive a few minutes early and introduce yourself politely
Send a short thank-you message afterward

precedence.why: Your practice answers are better when you understand the role.
You prepare answers before the interview day arrives.
Your outfit and route need to be planned before you go.
You send thanks after the interview has taken place.

templates.principle: Prepare for an interview by researching, planning, practicing, arriving early, and following up with thanks.

review.notes: Research and planning can happen in either order; alternates are professionally sound.
